THE PRESS ON THE ADHESION OF VIRGINIA.
From the Norfolk Virginian.

UNDER THE CROSSED SPEARS.
A great outrage has been inflicted on Virginia, and we have no honeyed words in which to hide the wrong, and no disposition to conceal our disgust at the violation of faith we have just witnessed. These are not the words of passionate temper, nor are they prompted by "a sudden heat." The compact made between the contracting parties—Congress and the President on one side, and the people of Virginia on the other—has been deliberately broken! and Virginia, after all her establishment, has been subjected to new humiliations. Under these circumstances, we look back at the recent past with profound regret, and forward to the future with sad abatement of our hopes for restored autonomy. There are those who will attribute these expressions of sorrow and disgust to our Bourbon philosophy but we do not stand alone in our opinions, nor are we peculiar in their expression.

THE Virginian then quotes from the Times and Tribune, of New York;

With these opinions from great Republican authorities, added to our own profound convictions, we may well be pardoned for declaring our disgust at the infraction of faith which we have suffered at the hands of Congress, and unhesitatingly put our opinion on record. There are those more sanguine of the future than we are, and dreamers may be sustained in their cheerful predictions. In the mean time we hope that the guns which are to be fired will be left untouched by the people. If we must march under the crossed spears of despotic and unconstitutional power, let us at least do it with decent composure and measured tread.

P.S. Since the above was written, "the salute" has been fired, and the patriotic artillerists have been informed by sable orators that Virginia may yet be remanded to a territorial condition if she does not behave herself. This is shame enough for one day, and we bow our head in sorrow at the dancing of these Helots of the State who, drunk on degradation, disport themselves before their masters.

From the New York Times.

The act of admission would have been more gracious had it been unencumbered with conditions which appear to reveal an exacting and suspicious temper, but which after all, are practically powerless. Of all the States which have regained fellowship in the Union under the terms of the reconstruction acts, not one presented itself with better title to unconditional and immediate recognition than Virginia. The grace of the recognition now accorded is marred by implied imputations upon the good faith of the people. What, under some circumstances might have been an outrage, is greatly mitigated by the fact that the provisos imposed will be virtually imperative. The bill as it has passed looks offensive, because clogged with conditions where all conditions are out of place. But they will neither hinder the restoration of the State nor lessen its usefulness, or retard its progress when restored. And bad as they seem to be, they are trifles compared with the tests which those who regard reconstruction simply as a partisan agency attempted to impose.

From the Boston Advertiser.

Looking at it in the light of policy, the new measure cannot fail to prove disastrous to the future prospects of the political minority in Virginia. The comparatively small number who will be shut out of the present Legislature are of no account. But they do not stand alone. They represent a great class in Virginia, bound together by common traditions, common experiences, and common retribution. The once active men who guided and controlled it have withdrawn in great measure from public life, but not from interest in public affairs. To them the new conditions are a fresh and needless humiliation. Human nature in Virginia must be of baser quality than exists in any other part of the world if it does not in some way compensate itself for these impositions in the future management of its affairs. It is the part of wisdom and craftsmanship to legislate for the future. Congress is in this matter legislating for the past, and is laying plans which, unless overruled for good, as so many of our short-sighted schemes heretofore have been, will bear bitter fruit for many years to come.

or of the school board in any town which has
abolished school districts therein, to notify such

thereof, and the names of the parents, guardians
or masters who ought to have supplied the
same.

to the next annual tax of such parents, guardians or masters, and the amount so added shall
be levied, collected and paid into the treasury of the
town or city taxes.

any parent, master or guardian, is unable to
pay the whole expense of the books so supplied
on his account, they shall omit to add the price
of such book or shall add only part thereof to
his annual tax, according to their opinion of his
ability to pay.

The vindication of the Secretary of State!
We publish below the report of the Committee appointed to examine the affairs of the Secretary of State, who were authorized to examine the affairs of the Secretary of State and report their Condition to the Senate. The report of the Committee is another one of those triumphant vindications of Republicans against the malignant assaults of the Democratic party. We say malignant assaults, because Mr. Winstead was pursued with unrelenting cruelty both in the public prints, and, as we are informed, upon the floor of the legislature. The Sentinel especially took occasion to use the most unjust rumors, gathered from various individuals, charging the Secretary with peculation and fraud, and many other things, which it is useless to recall here, although they have been extensively retailed, because they will now sink into the political sewer and soon pass away with the rest of such noisome garbage.

The following is the report referred to above:

The Committee appointed under the following resolutions, to-wit:—

Resolved, That Messrs. Winstead, Lindsay and Love be Committee authorized to examine the affairs of the Secretary of State; that they investigate his accounts for stationery, etc., compare his bills with his vouchers, in the office of the Treasurer of the State; compare his charges with the orders from the departments, examine the prices paid for stationery, and compare them with the wholesale prices of other houses dealing in the same articles, and if necessary, one of their number visit New York, to complete this investigation; also, that the Committee have power to send for persons and papers, and administer the oaths. Ratified 3rd day of Feb, 1870.

Have performed their duty, and respectfully report that they find nothing in the management of this department, under the existing laws, to disapprove. They find the Secretary of State well informed as to the duties of his Office; they find that further legislation is necessary in the management of the department of State, and report a bill with recommendations that it be passed. All of which is respectfully submitted.

C. S. WINSTEAD,

N. J. LINDSAY,

W. L. LOVE.
